# Sarabande (disambiguation)

The term "Sarabande" refers to several distinct and unrelated organizations across different creative industries. This disambiguation page provides detailed information on each entity to clarify the various subjects that may be referred to by this name. The most direct interpretation of the user query, "Sarabande (collection)," points to a specific fashion collection; however, the name is also used by a prominent literary press, a London-based arts foundation, and a long-standing American record label specializing in film scores. Each of these entities operates independently with unique histories, missions, and areas of influence.

## Sarabande Books

Sarabande Books is an award-winning, internationally-distributed, nonprofit independent literary publishing house headquartered in Louisville, Kentucky , . Founded in 1994 by Sarah Gorham and Jeffrey Skinner, the press is dedicated to creating "lasting editions that honor exceptional writing" , . It specializes in contemporary poetry, short fiction, and essays, often championing innovative, hybrid, and experimental forms that may be marginalized by for-profit publishers , . The press has built a catalog of nearly three hundred titles and is distributed nationally and internationally by Consortium Book Sales and Distribution (CBSD) , , . Its editorial leadership includes Kristen Renee Miller as Editor-in-Chief and Danika Isdahl as Managing Editor and Designer, who succeeded founder Sarah Gorham , . The press publishes between eight and twelve books annually and maintains a commitment to producing beautifully designed physical editions that remain in print , .

Sarabande Books' reputation is built upon its rigorous selection process and its support for emerging writers through prestigious annual competitions . These flagship contests include the Kathryn A. Morton Prize in Poetry, the Mary McCarthy Prize in Short Fiction, and The Sarabande Prize in the Essay , . Each prize offers a $2,000 advance and publication, and finalists are considered for publication regardless of winning , . The judging panels for these contests feature prominent figures in the literary world; for example, Ocean Vuong judged the 2024 poetry prize and Aimee Bender judged the 2024 fiction prize . The press also administers a chapbook prize and runs open submission periods during designated windows, requiring a $30 submission fee for contest entries , . All of its contests adhere to the Community of Literary Magazines and Presses (CLMP) Contest Code of Ethics, ensuring transparency and ethical judging processes , .

The list of authors published by Sarabande Books is distinguished by numerous accolades from the literary establishment, including Pulitzer Prize winners, National Book Award recipients, Guggenheim Fellows, and National Book Critics Circle Award winners , , . Notable works from its catalog demonstrate its commitment to diverse and formally innovative voices. For instance, Karisma Price's debut poetry collection, *I'm Always so Serious* (2023), received critical acclaim for its exploration of Black life in the United States and intergenerational trauma . Similarly, Corey Van Landingham’s poetry collection *Reader, I*, published in April 2024, was praised for its engagement with themes of marriage and selfhood , . Another critically lauded work is Lauren K. Watel’s *Book of Potions*, winner of the Kathryn A. Morton Prize, which was described by nine prominent poets as a masterpiece of sustained prose rhythm . The press continues to be an active force in contemporary literature, with recent publications including David Lawrence Morse's *The Book of Disbelieving* (2023) and upcoming titles like Kiki Petrosino's memoir *Bright* (2022) , . Beyond publishing, Sarabande Books serves as an educational resource through programs like the Sarabande Writing Labs and the Flo Gault Student Poetry Prize, supporting both emerging and established writers , .

## Sarabande Foundation

The Sarabande Foundation is a UK-based charitable organization founded in 2006 by the late fashion designer Lee Alexander McQueen , . Established with the vision of creating a fearless, non-hierarchical environment for artistic collaboration, the foundation continues to operate following McQueen's death in 2011 . It supports over 200 designers and artists through scholarships, studio spaces, and mentoring programs, explicitly distinguishing itself from commercial or editorial "collections" by focusing on nurturing individual creative talent , . The foundation fosters interdisciplinary collaboration among artists working in fields such as sculpture, painting, photography, weaving, and digital art , . In 2015, Trino Verkade, McQueen's first employee, founded another entity named the Sarabande Foundation in London, suggesting a continuation or evolution of McQueen's original vision, which is now celebrated as having created a model that other brands are beginning to replicate .

The foundation's headquarters and primary operational hub is located at 5 Carlos Place in Mayfair, London, where it operates studio spaces that have supported hundreds of artists . These studios host exhibitions showcasing works by supported artists and alumni, covering a wide range of media including jewellery, photography, painting, and sculpture , . The foundation actively engages with the public through curated events and residencies. A notable example is the "House of Bandits" residency held at Selfridges in London, which featured live studio spaces for rotating alumni artists, window installations recreating the studios of different creatives, and sales of limited-edition works by alumni and supporters like Thom Browne and Tim Burton , . In October 2023, the foundation hosted a pop-up event named 'House of Bandits' during Frieze Week, featuring emerging indie jewellery designers whose work drew inspiration from history, mythology, and biology .

Beyond providing resources for practicing artists, the Sarabande Foundation also focuses on community-building and career development. It hosts events like "What Now?", a post-college guide for recent graduates offering one-to-one advice, which attracted over 800 attendees in London and was scheduled to take place in New York in May 2024 . The foundation's community includes multidisciplinary artists such as NEWGEN award winner Arron Esh, who debuted at London Fashion Week, and Dean Hoy, a soft sculpture artist known for his "Bears Who Care" collaborations . While some sources indicate the foundation is headquartered in Haggerston, London, with a secondary site named 'Sarabande High Road', its primary base of operations and public-facing activities are centered in Mayfair , . Through its combination of practical support, public programming, and community engagement, the Sarabande Foundation serves as a living testament to Alexander McQueen's ethos of fostering visionary talent without hierarchical constraints.

## Varèse Sarabande

Varèse Sarabande is an American record label that specializes in motion picture and television soundtrack recordings , . Formed in 1978, the label was created through the merger of two separate companies: Tom Null's Sarabande Records and Chris Kuchler's Varèse International Records , , . The name itself is a composite, combining the surname of French-born composer Edgard Varèse with "sarabande," a slow Spanish dance form , . Initially established as an avant-garde classical music label, the merged entity pivoted its focus to film scores starting in June 1978, releasing its first soundtrack LP that year , . It became one of the world's largest producers of original motion picture score CDs during the 1980s and 1990s, reissuing rare or unavailable albums and releasing new works by artists no longer under contract , .

The label's historical significance lies in its crucial role as an archivist and curator of cinematic music history . By making classic film scores accessible to enthusiasts and scholars, Varèse Sarabande preserved a vital part of cultural heritage. A prime example is its 2004 restoration and reissue of Elmer Bernstein's iconic 1960 score for *The Magnificent Seven*, a Silver Age masterpiece that had become commercially scarce . Scholarly analysis confirms the label's importance, with academic texts on fantasy cinema citing its releases of scores by composers like Jerry Goldsmith (*The 7th Voyage of Sinbad*) and Tangerine Dream (*Legend*) as essential archival resources . Since its acquisition by Concord Music in February 2018, Varèse Sarabande has operated as a division of Concord's Craft Recordings imprint, continuing its legacy with a modern, collector-focused strategy , .

Today, Varèse Sarabande's product offerings emphasize high-quality, deluxe, and limited-edition physical media, particularly vinyl records . The label is known for producing special edition LPs, often pressed in exotic colored vinyl, accompanied by extensive liner notes written by noted journalists and artist essays . For example, its mid-to-late 2024 release slate included limited-run colored vinyl editions of scores by Hans Zimmer, Danny Elfman, Michael Giacchino, and Don Davis, each with strict worldwide print limits and a price point around $40 per title . This approach caters to collectors and dedicated fans, positioning the label as a premium purveyor of film music rather than a mass-market distributor. The label's catalog remains vast, encompassing thousands of soundtrack releases and continuing to issue new soundtracks for film and television , . The iconic inkblot logo, created by blowing a straw on India ink, is a recognizable symbol of its long history in the industry .

## Sarabande (Alexander McQueen collection)

The "Sarabande" collection refers to the Spring/Summer 2007 ready-to-wear fashion collection by the late British designer Alexander McQueen . Presented on a circular stage at the Cirque d’Hiver in Paris, the show was named after and inspired by the Baroque-era court dance of the same name, a slow and stately movement that contrasted with McQueen's typically frenetic energy , . The collection was widely acclaimed by critics as one of McQueen’s most beautiful and romantic works, hailed as evidence of his status as a "romantic genius" and elevating his reputation to a peak where commercial compromise was unnecessary . It served as a powerful commentary on the decay of beauty, achieved through deliberate, performative destruction of its central garment .

The aesthetic of the collection was Edwardian-inspired, featuring black-and-white ruffled gowns, tight hourglass-structured dresses, chiffon explosion skirts, and dusky pink silk corseted gowns adorned with spilling floral motifs . However, the collection's true centerpiece was a final showpiece dress named 'Sarabande' . Made from nude silk organza, this dress was meticulously embroidered with hundreds of real, frozen flowers . As the model walked down the runway, the flowers began to thaw and disintegrate, transforming the garment into a "living, dying, transient thing" , . This act of controlled decay embodied McQueen's recurring thematic preoccupations with transience, fragility, and the inevitable decline of beauty . The collection was so impactful that it directly spurred demand for bespoke bridal wear from brides and contributed foundational pieces to the 2011 landmark exhibition "Alexander McQueen: Savage Beauty" at The Metropolitan Museum of Art .

The 'Sarabande' dress was accessioned and documented by The Metropolitan Museum of Art in 2011, cementing its status as a significant piece of cultural and artistic history . Its inclusion in the museum's permanent archive alongside other iconic designs underscores its importance beyond mere haute couture. The collection as a whole solidified McQueen's position as a master of theatrical storytelling through fashion, where clothing becomes a vehicle for powerful narrative and emotion . The 'Sarabande' collection stands as a testament to his ability to blend exquisite craftsmanship with profound, often unsettling, artistic statements, leaving a lasting legacy in the annals of fashion history .

## Other Notable Uses of the Name

While the primary interpretations of "Sarabande" relate to the entities discussed previously, the name has been used in other contexts, most notably within the realm of contemporary classical music. One prominent example is the 2017 album *Black Sarabande* by British composer and pianist Robert Haigh, released on the New York-based Unseen Worlds label . This work consists of eleven tracks that blend piano melodies with electronics, thematically rooted in Haigh's childhood memories of a coal-mining village in South Yorkshire . The album is characterized by its hushed, Satie- and Harold Budd–influenced minimalism, use of discordant piano tones, ghostly overtones, and immersive, near-silent passages . Critical reception highlighted its atmospheric ambiguity and affective depth, situating it within the context of ambient and minimalist traditions and praising its evocation of imaginary rural landscapes . Unlike the other entities, which are organizations or a single fashion collection, *Black Sarabande* is a standalone musical composition, representing another distinct use of the name in the arts.

Another significant musical reference is the 1975 solo studio album titled *Sarabande* by English keyboardist and composer Jon Lord, best known as a member of the rock band Deep Purple . This album marked a departure from his rock-oriented work, featuring orchestral rock and progressive rock elements recorded with the Philharmonia Hungaria Orchestra conducted by Eberhard Schoener . The project brought together a stellar lineup of guest musicians, including Andy Summers before he joined The Police, and showcased Lord's compositional talents outside of his rock context . Reissued by Eagle Rock Entertainment, the album preserves its original dynamic range while enhancing audio clarity, demonstrating its continued relevance and appeal to listeners of symphonic and progressive rock . Like Haigh's album, Lord's *Sarabande* is a singular artistic work rather than the name of a collection or organization.

Furthermore, the name "Sarabande" appears in other cultural products, though these are less prominent in the provided sources. An example is the poetry collection *Reader, I* by Corey Van Landingham, published by Sarabande Books in 2024 , . While the book is published by the press, its title is a direct literary reference to Charlotte Brontë's *Jane Eyre* ("Reader, I married him"), indicating a thematic engagement with classic literature rather than a connection to the press's name . Similarly, Marianne Chan's 2024 poetry collection, *Leaving Biddle City*, published by Sarabande Books, uses a fictionalized name for her hometown, again showing the press's role as a publisher rather than a creator of titles . These examples illustrate that while "Sarabande" is a common name in the arts, it is often used as a component of a larger title or as the name of a specific work, rather than as a descriptor for a broader collection in the way the user's query implies. The most direct and unambiguous answer to the query remains Alexander McQueen's fashion collection.

## Comparative Analysis of Entities

To fully understand the multifaceted nature of the term "Sarabande," it is essential to compare and contrast the four primary entities identified: Sarabande Books, the Sarabande Foundation, Varèse Sarabande, and the Alexander McQueen collection. While they share a name, they are entirely independent in their founding, purpose, industry, and operational models. Their only common thread is the word "Sarabande" itself, which carries different connotations in each context.

The comparison reveals that the term "Sarabande" functions differently depending on the context. For Sarabande Books, "collection" refers to a curated volume of literary works, a standard publishing practice. For Varèse Sarabande, it refers to a compilation of musical compositions from a film, again a common industry term. The Alexander McQueen collection is the most literal use of the term, as it is a defined series of garments. The Sarabande Foundation, however, is the least likely candidate for being called a "collection"; its mission is to support individual artists, not to produce a curated set of products. Therefore, the user's query is most accurately answered by examining the McQueen collection, which is fundamentally a "collection" in the sense intended. The other entities are organizations that happen to share the name, but their operations and identities are distinct. This analysis confirms that there is no single entity named "Sarabande (collection)" beyond its application as a descriptor for the fashion line or as a general term for compilations in publishing and music.

The "Sarabande" collection featured black-and-white ruffled gowns, tight hourglass-structured dresses, chiffon explosion skirts, and dusky pink silk corseted gowns adorned with spilling floral motifs.
The "Sarabande" collection's true centerpiece was a final showpiece dress named 'Sarabande'.
The 'Sarabande' dress was made from nude silk organza.
The 'Sarabande' dress was meticulously embroidered with hundreds of real, frozen flowers.
As the model walked down the runway, the flowers on the 'Sarabande' dress began to thaw and disintegrate, transforming the garment into a "living, dying, transient thing".
This act of controlled decay embodied McQueen's recurring thematic preoccupations with transience, fragility, and the inevitable decline of beauty.
The "Sarabande" collection directly spurred demand for bespoke bridal wear from brides.
The "Sarabande" collection contributed foundational pieces to the 2011 landmark exhibition "Alexander McQueen: Savage Beauty" at The Metropolitan Museum of Art.
The 'Sarabande' dress was accessioned and documented by The Metropolitan Museum of Art in 2011.
The 'Sarabande' dress's inclusion in the museum's permanent archive alongside other iconic designs underscores its importance beyond mere haute couture.
The "Sarabande" collection as a whole solidified McQueen's position as a master of theatrical storytelling through fashion, where clothing becomes a vehicle for powerful narrative and emotion.

The 'Sarabande' collection stands as a testament to Alexander McQueen's ability to blend exquisite craftsmanship with profound, often unsettling, artistic statements, leaving a lasting legacy in the annals of fashion history.

1

Sarah Burton on Lee Alexander McQueen
-------------------------------------

![Image 1: woty](https://hips.hearstapps.com/hmg-prod/images/woty-1-1635421000.jpg?crop=1xw:1xh;center,top)

David Burton

"Every time I visit the studios at Sarabande, the air thrums with activity. The faint smell of oil paint lingers in the corridor as I watch a digital artist dancing, their body covered in sensors; around the corner, a woodcarver painstakingly chisels wooden tulips as sewing machines whirr. In the kitchen, the artists are talking, working things out together – forming their own smaller communities that will be their support system for years to come.

"In many ways, Sarabande represents the early Alexander McQueen studio in Hoxton Square, where I began my journey at McQueen 27 years ago. Like Sarabande, I remember the studio being alive with raw energy, passion and unfettered creativity.

"We were always looking for creatives in different disciplines; Lee never limited himself to working only with fashion people. I would hunt for a bedmaker to make the iron showpiece he had just envisioned, or a glassblower willing to attempt an impossibly fragile bodice for a model to wear. Lee loved the conversation between different visionaries and makers that all fed into making his dreams possible.

"Next year, the studios that were started by my friend, the brilliant Trino Verkade, will celebrate their 10-year anniversary. Trino was such a huge part of the birth and success of McQueen – she was his first employee – and she continues to work tirelessly to support every kind of creative. The foundation’s studios have helped hundreds of artists to further develop their passion into careers. The artists meet or are mentored by the best in the business – be that in fashion, art, film or jewellery. Lee loved women and this story shines a light on just a handful of the dozens of astounding, talented women that Sarabande has nurtured.

"The majority of those whom Sarabande has helped with studios have been artists, not fashion designers – sculptors, painters, performing and photographic artists... Lee had a place at Slade before he died. And this broad mix of creatives works its own kind of magic. It is fair to say that Sarabande Foundation created the model that other brands are now starting to replicate as they up studio spaces. I am in awe of the richness of the talent and I applaud its belief that success isn’t just commercial.

"Sarabande is a jewel, an incredibly special place where all individuals and ideas have importance, a home where everyone is supported and nurtured, and at the same time challenged to achieve their best. Sarabande is where dreams become reality. I am sure Lee would be very proud of it."

2

Michaela Yearwood-Dan, contemporary artist, on Harriet Horton
-------------------------------------------------------------

![Image 2: harriet horton, suzanne and i, 2015](https://hips.hearstapps.com/hmg-prod/images/harriet-horton-suzanne-and-i-2015-67051a4e4215a.jpg?crop=0.900101591601761xw:1xh;center,top)

Harriet Horton, Suzanne And I, (2015) - Courtesy of Sarabande

"I met Harriet while I was a resident at Sarabande. She was making taxidermy of creatures using neon lights and resin – beautiful, delicate pieces of prawns, octopus, birds; it was like a meeting of science and art. Now, she runs a shop and gallery in the Highlands, called Deluxe Miscellanea, with her partner Emma, who is also an artist. It’s a beautiful space in which she creates talismans and sculptures made from natural materials. Harriet and Emma invite creatives to pitch ideas around their practice. There is a shared meal that everyone pays to attend, then they all vote anonymously for the artist they think needs the money to develop their work. It reminds me of the way that Sarabande built a community. The art world is all very big-city-centred, so there’s something lovely about Deluxe Miscellanea existing in this ambient old mill at the edge of the country."

Advertisement - Continue Reading Below

3

Shona Heath, art director and set designer, on Jo Grogan
--------------------------------------------------------

![Image 3: jo grogan carving preliminary work sarabande foundation](https://hips.hearstapps.com/hmg-prod/images/jo-grogan-carving-preliminary-work-c-sarabande-foundation-67051bf5f3fb5.jpg?crop=1.00xw:0.800xh;0,0.101xh)

Jo Grogan carving preliminary work, courtesy of Sarabande Foundation.jpg

"I share a love of pattern and ornament, folk and the kitsch that Jo uses in her woodcarving. Wood is not a quick-result medium, and I praise her perseverance, especially as she creates intricate work. By choosing an ‘old craft’ that 3D printing could ‘replicate’, she continues the conversation between crafts with simple organic materials and human endeavour."

4

Gwendoline Christie, actress, on Judas Companion
------------------------------------------------

![Image 4: judas companion mask](https://hips.hearstapps.com/hmg-prod/images/judas-companion-mask-67051cf349e0a.jpg?crop=1.00xw:0.667xh;0,0.0454xh)

‘The English Patient’ (2022) by Judas Companion, courtesy of Sarabande

"I love that Judas Companion’s masks are wearable art. Imagine how transformed you’d be by wearing one – how it would completely change people’s attitudes to you and your experience of the world. Would it create fear or terror or fascination? What an alternative experience you could have, just slipping on this little pile of wool and crystal, beads and yarn.

"A particularly striking piece is a knitted orange mask with a bold, almost grotesquely wide mouth complete with diamond teeth. Is it a smile or a grimace? One eye is blind, the other is an open hole that you see the world out of if you’re wearing the mask or, if unworn, stands as an empty void. Where the other eye should be situated is a cluster of crystals, almost like coagulated blood – perhaps the eye has been gouged out? Maybe it never existed at all.

"There is a violence in this aesthetic that makes me think more deeply about what we’re seeing and experience an unconventional new beauty.Judas has now expanded her work to performance, painting and sculpture, and she uses ceramics in the masks and makes films. All initially inspired by Alexander McQueen!"

Advertisement - Continue Reading Below

5

Maggi Hambling, artist, on Laila Tara H
---------------------------------------

![Image 5: conjunction i and ii by laila tara h](https://hips.hearstapps.com/hmg-prod/images/conjunction-i-and-ii-by-laila-tara-h-c-bjdeakinphotography-4853-67051e6b976fb.jpg?crop=0.825xw:1.00xh;0.0901xw,0)

Conjunction I and II by Laila Tara H, BJ Deakin Photography, Courtesy of Sarabande-

"There are two works from a recent show that I read as a diptych, each work titled _Conjunction (I and II)_. As an art student in the 1960s in London, I would visit the British Museum and study Chinese and Japanese landscape and ink works on paper: I strongly identify with the belief that where one does not touch the surface is as important as where one does. Laila's work embodies this discipline, amplifying the inherent conflict they depict - the woman and flames in _Conjunction I_ and the escape to peace in _Conjunction II_. Artists often try to say more with more...as I get older, I try to say more with less. One should always approach a work of art in silence, and imagination is crucial: Laila's work allows one the space to imagine, with a mediative rhythm that also resonates with the work of Agnes Martin, a great master whom I admire._"_

6

Kate Bryan, chief art director of Soho House, on Darcey Fleming
---------------------------------------------------------------

![Image 6: yellow shag char by darcey fleming, sarabande](https://hips.hearstapps.com/hmg-prod/images/unknown-1-670521103f095.jpg?crop=1xw:1xh;center,top)

Yellow Shag Chair by Darcey Fleming, courtesy of Sarabande

"Darcey’s art is so avant garde; I was floored by her originality when I first walked into her studio. I love the way it disrupts the historic tradition of weaving by using baler twine – this discarded material mostly used by farmers – and turning it into something precious, in bright yellow and green. Within 10 minutes of seeing her work, I commissioned her to create a huge installation at Soho Farmhouse. It will be the biggest piece in our collection.

"Watching her create has been so inspiring she is so meticulous and was clearly born to be an artist."

Advertisement - Continue Reading Below

7

Sandy Powell, film costume designer, on Daisy Collingridge
----------------------------------------------------------

![Image 7: burt](https://hips.hearstapps.com/hmg-prod/images/daisy-collingridge-with-sandy-powell-c-sarabande-foundation-670522926b987.jpg?crop=0.6673728813559322xw:1xh;center,top)

Darren Gerrish

"When I met Burt, I was immediately struck by him, so I sat next to him to talk. Burt is one of Daisy’s creations – a pink, wearable work of art – and it turned out that Daisy was inside. Daisy studied womenswear at Central Saint Martins, but was always more interested in fabric than fashion. She likes the idea of bodies that aren’t the same as your own; showing the inside and the outside at the same time – realising that we’re all the same underneath. Her work isn’t typically pretty, although, of course, I find it beautiful."

8

Sam Taylor-Johnson, film director and artist, on Kasia Wozniak
--------------------------------------------------------------

![Image 8: kasia wozniak](https://hips.hearstapps.com/hmg-prod/images/kasiawozniak-for-sarabande-mcqueen-voss-2023-6705236780fb3.jpg?crop=1.00xw:0.835xh;0,0.0823xh)

‘Voss’ (2023) by Kasia Wozniak, courtesy of Sarabande

"I hadn’t seen anyone use the wet-plate collodion process \[an early photographic practice\] in a large format for a long time. Kasia’s work was so good that I let her know via Instagram that I thought her photographs were truly arresting. They look as though they could be from the 1930s, yet there’s something a little modern about them as well. They’re mysterious. When you take a portrait and the process of it isn’t so immediate, it creates a different texture on the surface, and an atmosphere around what’s photographed.

"In this era in which everyone’s a photographer, to use a still and lengthy process is such a perfect idea – a step back to composition technique, and being thoughtful and slow. The subjects would have had to sit very still, and just ponder the moment. I’d love to commission one because I think they’re so special."

Advertisement - Continue Reading Below

9

Hikari Yokoyama, founder of the design studio Naum House, on Hannah Norton
--------------------------------------------------------------------------

![Image 9: kingswood hannah norton](https://hips.hearstapps.com/hmg-prod/images/kingswood-c-hannah-norton-6705248e07d98.jpg?crop=1.00xw:0.801xh;0,0.137xh)

Kingswood, Hannah Norton, courtesy of Sarabande

"Hannah Norton primarily works with communities of people who are underrepresented in the cultural landscape, and her subjects piqued my curiosity – who is the person, where are they from, what are they feeling, what does it say about society today? It’s true storytelling through the photographic medium."

10

Maria Balshaw, director of Tate, on Clara Pinto
-----------------------------------------------

![Image 10: clara pinto coat](https://hips.hearstapps.com/hmg-prod/images/3-clara-pinto-photographer-francesco-zinno-670525faf3559.jpg?crop=1.00xw:0.801xh;0,0.102xh)

Clara Pinto AW 2024 /Photographer Francesco Zinno

"I’m always interested in the interface between fashion and design and fine art. Clara caught my eye via the discovery lab that London Fashion Week does in partnership with Sarabande – her wool clothes looked to me like sculpture.

"The first piece I saw was a marvellous black coat with sleeves in a cape shape. She uses a felting technique to pull various colours of wool through, so it’s very abstract interms of its pattern. It made me think of the amazing womenartists who recreate the female form in subversive ways,often using textiles, such as Sarah Lucas or Louise Bourgeois.

"I also see her as a practitioner who has a lot in common with contemporary indigenous makers, who view the traditions that they inherit and the world through the long lens of sustainability. So, Clara takes traditional Argentinian practices and uses them for a contemporary end. She embraces the cutting edge of technology to enhance textile design, but for grounded, sustainable reasons, and draws on the past while thinking powerfully into the future."

Advertisement - Continue Reading Below

11

Sadie Coles, founder of Sadie Coles HQ, on Rachel Fleming Hudson
----------------------------------------------------------------

![Image 11: football hooligans](https://hips.hearstapps.com/hmg-prod/images/football-hooligans-costume-and-image-by-rachel-fleminger-hudson-670527068dbd1.jpg?crop=0.7501272264631044xw:1xh;center,top)

Football Hooligans costume and image by Rachel Fleminger-Hudson, courtesy of Sarabande

"I like the time-travelling aspect of Rachel's work: her image of football fans is a disconcertingly accurate recreation of my life in the Seventies. It captures the all-consuming feeling of being in a teenage gang, the intense connection, the passionate obsession and the sartorial signalling. Everything then, from clothes and hairstyles to feminism and politics, was home-made, goofy and  
hopeful.

"What is interesting is that the photographs are created now. They are performative, the opposite of documentary: a restaging that is ultimately theatre. Painstakingly crafted images like this are  
especially compelling in a time when AI and the internet have had such an impact on authenticity."

12

Trino Verkade, Sarabande Founder, on Saelia Aparico
---------------------------------------------------

![Image 12: fumi gallery](https://hips.hearstapps.com/hmg-prod/images/low-res-fumi-gallery-image-6705286335163.jpg?crop=0.668xw:1.00xh;0.151xw,0)

Saelia Aparicio (Picture by Tom Hartford, courtesy of FUMI gallery and the artist)

"Saelia applied for a Sarabande studio in 2016. Initially, she presented multiple sculptures showing the extent of her work, which included glass-blowing, wood sculptures and powerful and arresting murals, which she paints freehand with a skill that is mind-blowing. But my favourite pieces are the anthropomorphic women stools she created here. Each series animates individual women, they are multicultural and, as they stack together, their unity gives a feeling of a tower of strength. Saelia continues to create work that is challenging and sometimes awkward for the viewer, but always engaging - there is almost a childlike fascination with form and the human body. Her pieces show us the beauty of the world hidden behind a twisted, strange, but charming viewpoint."

_Cementing its reputation as London’s best boulevard for fashion and fine art, Mayfair’s ever-elegant Mount Street is hosting a week-long celebration of culture and creativity, where cross-disciplinary conversation is encouraged. Swing by talks and pop-up events at Erdem, Marni or Toteme en route to 5 Carlos Place, which Alexander McQueen’s art foundation Sarabande is taking over to showcase the jewellery, photography, painting and sculptures made by the artists it supports – including the 11 rising stars profiled in Bazaar Art._

_Mount Street Neighbourhood Arts Festival runs until 12 October. For more information, visit mayfairldn.com_

3.content:
From human hair to woven leather and precious metals, Sarabande Foundation's latest exhibition _WARPED_ has it all. Marking the end of the capital's annual London Craft Week event, the two-day-only show acts as a celebration of the art of contemporary weaving while paying homage to the significance of the loom - an integral instrument to the functionings of fabric (and, therefore, society), but also one that has remained relatively unchanged over hundreds of years.

Opening at Sarabande on Friday, 12 May, the immersive exhibition will showcase the talents of three Sarabande studio residents whose weaving work will stand tall next to an eight x two metre loom installation produced by Souvenir Scenic Studios and designed by the three spotlighted artists. Featuring talents [Megan Brown](http://www.meganbrownjewellery.com/), jewellery designer [Anouska Samms](http://www.anouskasamms.com/), who is an interdisciplinary designer and leather weaver-cum-fashion designer [Martina Spetlova](http://www.martinaspetlova.com/), _WARPED_ will showcase the artists' own unique approaches to weaving and their peculiar use of materials. All we'll say is expect the unexpected as a biomedicine degree comes in handy for one designer, while an all too familiar weaving archive over 180 years old becomes useful to another; throw in the unassuming association between human hair resembling mother-daughter relations, and hey presto: you have _WARPED._ Read on to find out more about the three artists, their practice and what makes them tick.

I hope 'WARPED' inspires visitors to see weaving in a new light, as a dynamic and versatile art form that has the power to transform any material into a work of art' - Megan Brown, jewellery designer

![Image 1](https://cms.showstudio.com/images/nN02vOngeC5Rd3yeZgdbgbWXrzg=/517525/width-30/draped_earrings_photographed_by_StueyB.jpg)

Draped earrings by Megan Brown. Photographed by Stuey'B

Jewellery artist Megan Brown isn't the first in her family to go into the jewellery trade; she's, in fact, following in the footsteps of someone she's related to but never met - her great, great grandfather Herbert Brown, who set up a jewellers and weaving company over 180 years ago. 'Through my work, I explore the interplay of soft, flowing fabric and hard, durable metal,' Brown tells me, using these woven contradictions to 'capture the delicate beauty of one in the enduring strength of the other'. Brown's speciality lies in mimicking the fluid movement of textiles in her sculpted pieces - whether hand-woven jewellery designs or one-of-a-kind silver sculptures. Get to know her below.

![Image 2](https://cms.showstudio.com/images/33DQnSZNJJao9fJofzffd__epYw=/517508/width-30/Portait_Photographed_by_StueyB.jpg)

Megan Brown

**Christina Donoghue: What does the term 'craft' mean to you? What do you think the importance of craft is in the 21st century?**

**Megan Brown:** I once heard someone say that craft is the process of tuning the spark of an idea into something tangible by using your own hands; this, I feel, sums up what 'craft' means to me. Its modern importance comes from providing a valuable counterbalance amidst our fast-paced, technology-driven world; it reminds us of the importance of taking time to create and appreciate things made by hand. Moreover, craft also connects us to our heritage, allowing us to tap into the wisdom and traditions of previous generations.

**CD: You're very transparent about your business being inspired by your great-great grandfather's work 180 years ago. Can you remember a lightbulb moment when this known fact directly inspired your own path?**

**MB:** I've known about my family's textile mill for as long as I can remember. It's something my mum and dad were always eager to share with us all, as it's an integral part of our heritage. But honestly, it wasn't until recently that I truly understood how much of an impact it had on me. During lockdown, I began working on a new jewellery collection to represent my identity as a designer better. The designs I had created up until then had always been very sculptural, with a strong focus on flowing lines. It dawned on me that what I was drawing was fundamentally a weaving - consider this my lightbulb moment - as it dawned on me that my family's legacy has been influencing my own path without me even realising it. It's a powerful reminder of the importance of heritage and tradition and how they can shape who we are and what we create.

![Image 3](https://cms.showstudio.com/images/Xo8T5CgAFdXsHArehOxKX_bL6B8=/517511/width-30/Hasir_Hoops_Photography_by_Camille_Liu.jpg)

'Hasir Hoops' by Megan Brown. Photography by Camille Liu

**CD: Do you feel the acceleration of technology is hindering craft in the UK?**

**MB:** While some might argue that technology threatens traditional craft practices here in the UK, I believe it can be a powerful tool for innovation and experimentation. With the help of modern technology, artisans have access to a whole new range of materials, techniques, and tools that would have been unimaginable only just a few decades ago. This not only opens up new possibilities for creative expression but also allows artisans to refine their skills and techniques in exciting new ways. Technology also has the potential to make craft more accessible to a wider audience, breaking down barriers of geography and distance. Through online platforms and digital media, artisans can showcase their work to a global audience and connect with like-minded makers from around the world. In short, I see technology as a powerful enabler of craft, one that has the potential to unlock new levels of creativity and collaboration in the UK and beyond.

**CD: What do you want the viewer to take away from** **_WARPED_****?**

**MB:** I hope _WARPED_ inspires visitors to see weaving in a new light, as a dynamic and versatile art form that has the power to transform any material into a work of art. By showing the work of three distinctly different artists and designers using weaving as part of their practice, we hope to give an insight into the boundless creativity of weavers and designers worldwide. Ultimately, I hope that, ultimately, visitors to _WARPED_ will walk away with a newfound appreciation for the beauty and complexity of weaving, and perhaps even be inspired to try their own hand at this time-honoured craft.

Craft is the process of tuning the spark of an idea into something tangible - Megan Brown

![Image 4](https://cms.showstudio.com/images/ZHzMWWl9-VaOEzu5uJAg7qW88Ss=/517512/width-30/twin_vessels_photo_by_Anouska_Samms.jpeg)

'Twin vessels' by Anouska Samms. Photography by artist

Anouska Samms is obsessed with hair. Whether it be hair on your head or the grotesque nature many have towards body hair once it's no longer attached to us. Using clay and human hair to create what she refers to as dysfunctional containers (sculptures), Samms intricately observes mother-daughter relationships, using her own maternal connections as a starting point for research. 'There's a matrilineal connection across five generations of women in my family through a seemingly unquestioned ritual of dying their hair red, like a strange form of "mother-imitation"', Samms informs. 'Even if they didn't get on at times, there was this unspoken desire and act where everyone just ended up expressing themselves similarly through their hair.' Considering this her starting point, least to say, Samms isn't afraid to admit all her friends are hairdressers - where else is she to collect hair samples from, after all? Get to know her here.

![Image 5](https://cms.showstudio.com/images/T_rpNmynYgvPoOyAtkphjBStLj4=/517509/width-30/Anouska_Samms_Studio.jpeg)

Anouska Samms

**CD: What does the word 'craft' mean to you?**

**AS:** This is tricky because I feel it's hard to hold onto your own opinion when the meaning of craft - or rather its status - changes over a number of years within the culture itself. Like anything, it comes in cycles where the fashion and art worlds re-embrace craft in a notable way which is ultimately a great thing. On the flip side, I spoke to a curator recently who reminded me what we considered to be craft ten or so years ago has radically changed. For example, and quite rightly, the distinction between art and craft is ever the more blurred, as illustrated in recent mainstream art shows such as Hayward Gallery's _Strange Clay_ and the current [Tate Modern retrospective of Magdalena Abakanowicz's](https://www.tate.org.uk/whats-on/tate-modern/magdalena-abakanowicz?gad=1&gclid=Cj0KCQjwpPKiBhDvARIsACn-gzA9nGI3fXgATN2ePQmIwAnYPV0WRjdN66Txd9ey33Vi4jwi-e8_0BkaAheFEALw_wcB) incredible woven work. But I don't know if 'craft' ever really loses its silly stigma in the art world. If it had, perhaps we wouldn't still hear the tired old question of 'is it craft, or is it art and design?' in relation to a piece of work. For me, traditional craft is something I adopt in my own work because it lends itself to the art I create with it.

**Christina Donoghue: Where and how did the idea of weaving hair with ceramics come from?**

**AS:** Each technique and form I use tend to have a meaning. When looking at mother-daughter relationships - which is what my work deals with - hair, weaving, and clay are extremely symbolic. Mitochondrial DNA is found within the hair shaft and is passed down to a child from their mother or pregnant parent. This is further emphasised when I weave the hair, as weaving represents the universal mythic trope whereby the warp and weft symbolise the tissues of a child's body woven into the womb of a pregnant parent. Clay, transformative matter that inherits the quality of the ground it is removed from, can create vessels from the ceremonial to the mundane. So I like to play on this idea of the ceremonial form in a humorous way when exploring the ways my own family have made a very literal expression of their bond. I tend to make strange vessel-like structures, playing with the idea of mother and daughter relationships through the form of the 'sacred vessel'. Both hair and clay as two organic materials that are endlessly malleable.

![Image 6](https://cms.showstudio.com/images/ZwcNIo04l6QJ-2GzNRz8kpP_hkY=/517513/width-30/CROPPED_CLOSE-UP__of_Big_Mother_by_Anouska_Samms_photo_by_Gareth_Williams.jpg)

'Big Mother' by Anouska Samms. Photography by Gareth Williams

**CD: Has your own process of referencing mother-daughter relationships in your work impacted your own?**

**AS:** I completed a short experimental documentary last year titled, _It's Not Perverse, It's Mothers_, which I found both challenging and healing, but overall, I would say it impacted the relationships I have with both my mother and grandmother for the better, so yes. The film explored the same hair-dying ritual I examine in my sculptures and tapestries.

**CD: To state the obvious, society has quite a complicated relationship to hair, especially when it doesn't just appear on one's head... Does this tricky relationship serve any inspiration to you and your connection with your own sculptural works?**

**AS:** Yes! Anthropologist Emma Tarlo talks about this in her book, [_Entanglement: The Secret Life of Hair_](https://www.amazon.co.uk/Entanglement-Secret-Lives-Emma-Tarlo/dp/1780749929), particularly how once human hair is disembodied, it can often take on a new meaning and create very visceral responses. Seeing strands of hair detached from someone's head - perhaps left on the bathroom floor - can then be viewed as grotesque. But before, when it was on someone's head, it's likely that it didn't ignite the same response. In my work, I like to think that the delicate and ornate details are subverted by the presence of the abject in the use of disembodied human hair. From the outside, my work can look like thread, but when closely examined, the same piece of work can then provoke different feelings once people recognise it for what it actually is. For me, I like to play with this in a tongue-in-cheek way to represent the purity and absurdity of the mother and daughter exchange. When you take a closer look at the relationship, different layers are revealed.

![Image 7](https://cms.showstudio.com/images/R7vn1-wVTldvjdrRxsuTk3iyFWo=/517514/width-30/a_close_up_of_Big_Mother_tapestry.jpeg)

A photo of 'Big Mother' tapestry, Anouska Samms

**CD: Am I correct in assuming you're also a filmmaker?**

**AS:** I studied film production at university as I thought I wanted to work in the film industry due to my love and appreciation for storytelling. Apart from taking a few ceramics classes here and there, I'm self-taught regarding my actual sculptural work. Storytelling is still something integral to my practice, realised through my use of materials and techniques, but I must say, it would appear that every couple of years or so I make a film; there are some ideas that need to be communicated differently and filmmaking provides that outlet for me. I once heard a comedian say, 'when dealing with complex memories of feelings, when you can turn them into a different form - whether that be through a book or another work of art - you can then make those feelings into a type of literal thing, and once they exist in a new way, they can be physically shared and live outside of your own body'. This really resonated with me, especially when I completed the _It's Not Perverse, It's Mothers_ documentary. Once my feelings existed in a different form, I dropped a lot of concerns that I previously had and was able to become a better daughter.

**What do you want the audience to take away from** **_WARPED_****?**

**AS:** Through the loom installation designed by all three of us, _WARPED_ pays homage to the design of a machine that has remained relatively unchanged through time and geography. Through the two-day exhibition, we want to show visitors the innovative and experimental ways the common loom can still be used today.

![Image 8](https://cms.showstudio.com/images/HshkFrqMP6UdNIGhigKJubhPKrE=/517515/width-30/Soho_Home_chair_cover_credits_MS_lEmmYjt.jpg)

Soho Home chair cover, Martina Spetlova

What hair is to Samms, colour is to Spetlova; the Czech-born designer would struggle to imagine a life without it. Her USP is the rich hues of canary yellow, royal blue and crimson reds clashing to create a look-at-me piece to be modelled by any wearer confident enough. Only working with European tanneries using metal-free leather, her designs - often jackets - embrace both handcrafting traditions and sustainability. 'I am also a big believer in storytelling and transparency', she tells me. Fascinated by the in-between narrative that can surround a product, her pieces have 'a chip embedded in them reviewing materials, sourcing and processes, inviting my clients to interact with my work in a more meaningful way.' Sounds quite science-based, doesn't it? Well, now would be the appropriate time to tell you Spetlova is also a bio-medicine graduate. Of course, she is. Get to know her below.

![Image 9](https://cms.showstudio.com/images/Na4XDt3GW9X8dcuBfRBxzMHZ29o=/517510/width-30/MS_Portrait.jpg)

Martina Spetlova

**CD: What does the word ‘craft’ mean to you?**

**MS:** Craft is about taking the time to learn and master a skill and then using that skill to create something beautiful. It requires patience, persistence, and a willingness to experiment and is a process that is often slow and deliberate, but the end result is something that is unique, personal, and imbued with the care and attention of the maker. For me, it is also about innovation and pushing the boundaries of what is possible with a given material or technique. It involves taking risks, exploring new ideas, and finding ways to bring creativity and beauty to everyday objects.

**Christina Donoghue: What importance do you think weaving has in contemporary culture?**

**Martina Spetlova:** Weaving is a traditional craft that is being revitalised and reinterpreted by artists and designers worldwide. It offers a sense of connection between the maker and the material and is a slow and deliberate process that requires attention to detail and a deep understanding of the properties of the materials being used. This creates a sense of mindfulness and intentionality that is often lacking in our fast-paced, disposable culture. It is also a way to create beautiful and environmentally responsible textiles, which has become increasingly important in contemporary culture as we seek ways to reduce our impact on the planet. Weaving also has cultural significance and is often tied to specific traditions and communities. By incorporating weaving into contemporary design, we can help to preserve and celebrate these traditions while also introducing them to a wider audience.

![Image 10](https://cms.showstudio.com/images/yNgEDGrdEWeIHxhdmHUBCBhA-Hs=/517518/width-30/Patchwork_wall_paneling_credits_ms.jpg)

Patchwork wall paneling, Martina Spetlova

**CD: It's documented that you have a chemistry degree and see subtle similarities in how you conduct chemical experiments and approach your textiles...**

**MS:** Yes, my background in chemistry has definitely influenced my approach to textile design. I see many similarities between the process of conducting chemical experiments and the process of creating textiles. Both involve a great deal of trial and error and the ability to manipulate materials in new and creative ways. For example, in both fields, you have to think carefully about the properties of materials and how they will react with other substances. It's all about experimentation and finding new and innovative ways to work with materials.

**CD: Who is the character you imagine wearing your clothes?**

**MS:** I design for a confident, independent, and adventurous person. My clothes are for someone who appreciates the beauty of handmade textiles and unique, sustainable, and high-quality pieces. The character I imagine wearing my clothes is someone who is unafraid to stand out and express themselves through what they wear. I also love when my pieces become everyday jackets you throw on rather than occasionwear.

![Image 11](https://cms.showstudio.com/images/uSMgbwNBYfdI2MmKTuum-3NByPg=/517516/width-30/Soho_House_collab_credits_MS.jpg)

Soho House collaboration, Martina Spetlova

**CD: I've read somewhere that you sometimes showcase your collections through the medium of fashion film; what is it about this art form that has attracted you to it?**

**MS:** I love the medium of film as it allows me to showcase my pieces in a more dynamic and immersive way. It offers a way to bring the clothes to life and create a visual narrative around them, which can be very powerful. Film allows me to tell a story with my designs and convey the inspiration behind them in a way that is not always possible with still images. The last time I experimented with moving image was in collaboration with the 3D animated film director duo [THOMASZEWICZ STUDIO](https://www.tomaszewicz.co.uk/). They produced a wonderfully abstract film that resonated visually and emotionally with my brand and audience.

**CD: What do you want the audience to take away from** **_WARPED_****?**

**MS:** I want visitors to see the potential for innovation and creativity within this traditional technique.

I also want to convey the importance of sustainability and ethical sourcing in the textile industry. Through my work, I hope to raise awareness about the impact of fashion and textiles on the environment and the people involved in the production process.

Lastly, I want to challenge preconceived notions of what fashion and design can be and how by combining unexpected materials, colours, textures and technology, we can push the boundaries of 'traditional' fashion weaving and appreciate the beauty and artistry that goes into creating handmade textiles.

![Image 12](https://cms.showstudio.com/images/FIyrAvnERT1T0rIyQ1MnpIMJBbA=/517517/width-30/Sylwana_Zybura_photography_Tomas_C_Toth_Styling.jpg)

Design by Martina Spetlova. Photography by Sylwana Zybura

_Black Sarabande_
=================

[Robert Haigh](https://pitchfork.com/artists/24427-rob-haigh/)

2020

![Image 3: Image may contain Plant and Cactus](https://media.pitchfork.com/photos/5e289c0325643f00082b2e8c/1:1/w_450%2Cc_limit/Black%2520Sarabande_Robert%2520Haigh.jpg)

7.6

By [Andy Beta](https://pitchfork.com/staff/andy-beta/)

*   Genre:
    
    Experimental
    
*   Label:
    
    Unseen Worlds
    
*   Reviewed:
    
    January 27, 2020
    

This contemporary classical pianist’s music proves more unsettling the more you disturb its placid surface. 

Save this story

Save this story

Depending on what release you discovered first, you might have believed there were two different Robert Haighs operating in the UK during the 1980s and ’90s. There was the pianist and composer who worked with [Nurse With Wound](https://pitchfork.com/artists/3079-nurse-with-wound/) and released elegant modern classical albums like 1987’s _Valentine Out of Season_. But what to make of the Robert Haigh behind the neck-whipping jungle breakbeats of the Omni Trio, a force throughout the drum ’n’ bass era in the UK? As that project drew to a close in the early 2000s, the more contemplative side of Haigh reemerged with a string of contemporary classical albums. They made for a perfect fit for New York’s Unseen Worlds label; his 2017 album _Creatures of the Deep_ slotted well alongside pianists new and old, ranging from “Blue” Gene Tyranny to [Lubomyr Melnyk](https://pitchfork.com/artists/5407-lubomyr-melnyk/) to [Leo Svirsky](https://pitchfork.com/artists/leo-svirsky/).

Haigh’s _Black Sarabande_ explores terrain similar to _Deep_, mixing gorgeous piano melodies with a patina of electronics. But where that previous album evoked the properties of water, _Sarabande_ feels grounded. It draws on Haigh’s childhood memories of UK coal country and the hardscrabble “pit village” of Worsbrough in South Yorkshire where he was raised. There’s a heavy atmosphere to these 11 tracks, never wholly enveloped in blackness but always threatened to tip over into it.

The opening title track is hushed, provoking comparisons to [Harold Budd](https://pitchfork.com/artists/8602-harold-budd/) or Erik Satie. Yet as Haigh’s struck keys hover in space, they turn slightly discordant, like a chill settling into the skin. “Stranger on the Lake” strikes a balance between piano and electronics to luminous effect, its melody shadowed by ghostly overtones. Midway through, the ambient haze swells, and when it finally recedes, the piece is suffused with harp plucks and electronics, making you feel like you’ve left one piece behind and emerged in another one entirely.

_Black Sarabande_’s calm surface proves illusory the more listens you give it. Struck piano wires startle the surface of the otherwise-placid “Wire Horses”; a gush of strings arrives and just as quickly disappears into the woozy, fluttering ambience of “Painted Serpent.” There are moments when Haigh’s playing verges on silence, so that if you’re listening on earbuds, you might hear your own footsteps through the snow more loudly than the music. The gorgeous and brief “Air Madeleine” sounds as if you’re walking around a frozen pond in the countryside and seated next to Haigh on the creaky piano bench all at once, as imaginary a landscape (and interior) as anything [Brian Eno](https://pitchfork.com/artists/526-brian-eno/) could have conceived.

	Jon LordSarabandeReview by Larry Toering
At the moment there is much to be said on behalf of  Jon Lord, who recently earned an honorary degree, has been very busy recording and playing live since leaving Deep Purple at the turn of the century. As I write this he is fighting for his life against cancer, so the support for one of our heroes is in order. He has been around since the beginning and played with all of the greats, from McCartney and Harrison, to Hendrix and Blackmore, to Wakeman and Satriani - the list is endless. He is as good as they come, whether playing hard rock in Deep Purple, or classic on his own, and sometimes with them, he is without a doubt a true original. On this Eagle Rock re-issue of Sarabande, there is just enough clarity added without flattening the ebbing waves of sound to be heard throughout this great album with the Philharmonia Hungaria Orchestra, conducted by Eberhard Schoener. This includes great tracks, all of them with a variety of styles blended together - long symphonic pieces of prog candy. Joining Lord and symphony, are Mark Nauseef and Pete York on drums and percussion, Paul Karass on bass and Andy Summers on guitar.(before he joined the Police) This has always been a favorite Lord solo album of mine, an ascending work of art, and it stands the test of time, as the Doctor himself does. He is a humbly gifted and gentle wise man, who has given generations of music to the world in the name of peace, love and prosperity.
This review is  available in book format (hardcover and paperback)                                                         in                               Music        Street         Journal:     2011      Volume 5  at lulu.com/strangesound.

	Track by Track Review

	Fantasia
Orchestral bombast sets things up for a minute or so, before two and a half minutes of pure beauty fades into a roaring frenzy. This is very heavy handed but accessible because it's so commanding, but, then what else can one expect from such a piece, as the orchestra takes full control of things?

	SarabandeA soothing, almost jazzy rhythm section sends Summers into recognition and things could not be more pleasant. Everything just goes together so well as Lord sails away with some seriously tasty synth work. Things aren't anywhere near over though, as Lord and Summers then go into some nice interplay and out of nowhere comes a lovely orchestral arrangement of majestic proportions to wrap it all up. This is an absolutely epic number, an underrated masterpiece.

	AriaNext is this lovely piano ballad, a massively infectious work of art, with Lord at his lighthearted best, sparring with a light string arrangement, but only for texture here. It is brilliant, melodic and classy.

	GigueThis is probably the most versatile, accessible and most well known number on the album. Both Lord and Summers shine along with Nauseef at his percussive best, and there’s a bass line that won't quit.

	BoureeThis is another one that just about has it all, with a lot of percussion beginning things, and this takes Lord into percussion mode himself by perfectly blending in with a heavy bottom groove. Again it's yet another interesting number with all kinds of things going on from tribal beats to classical motifs.

	PavaneProbably the most classical performance from Lord himself on the album, this is another masterpiece of movie soundtrack sort of music. This is not a bad thing and often recognized in Lord's more classical work.

	CapriceThis is an uplifting one to say the least, after that... it's a comical little gem with Lord all over the place, showing an almost Beatles sort of humor. Things really are cooking by now and there is no secret to the quality of music in each and every song on this fantastic time piece.

	FinaleStarting and ending with a grand salvo, all kinds of cool tid bits float around in-between on this magnificent closer. It just tops the whole work of wonder off in style. I don't think the curious will be stopping at one listen to this prog heavy needle in the haystack, which features a killer performance by Andy Summers.
